clinicalPearls: Caused by loss-of-function variants in the urate transporters URAT1 (SLC22A12) or GLUT9 (SLC2A9), leading to renal urate wasting
Defined biochemically by a low serum uric acid with an inappropriately high fractional excretion of urate
Most individuals are asymptomatic and identified incidentally on a low serum urate
The classic complication is exercise-induced acute kidney injury, typically after intense anaerobic exertion
Urate stones and haematuria are the other recognised complications from heavy urinary urate excretion
Management is preventive: avoiding strenuous anaerobic exercise, maintaining good hydration, and considering antioxidant strategies around exertion
GLUT9 defects tend to cause more profound hypouricaemia and a higher complication risk than URAT1 defects
reference.pathophysiology: URAT1 and GLUT9 are the principal transporters mediating reabsorption of filtered urate in the proximal tubule; URAT1 exchanges urate across the apical membrane while GLUT9 returns urate to the blood across the basolateral membrane. Loss of either transporter impairs urate reabsorption, so a large fraction of filtered urate is excreted, producing a low serum concentration with a high fractional excretion. The heavy urinary urate load predisposes to crystal formation, stones, and haematuria. Exercise-induced acute kidney injury is thought to arise because urate is an important circulating antioxidant, and its deficiency, combined with exertional generation of reactive oxygen species, promotes renal vasoconstriction and tubular injury.
additionalDifferentials: Acquired urate wasting in malignancy or liver disease
Dietary or laboratory causes of low measured urate
additionalInvestigations: Serum uric acid demonstrating persistent hypouricaemia
Fractional excretion of urate showing inappropriately high renal loss
Renal function testing during and after episodes of exercise-induced injury
Renal ultrasound for urate stones or nephrocalcinosis
redFlags: Acute kidney injury following intense exercise, often with loin pain
Obstructing urate calculi or gross haematuria
Recurrent episodes of exertional renal impairment
reference.prognosis: Long-term outlook is usually good with preventive measures, and baseline renal function is typically normal; however, recurrent exercise-induced acute kidney injury or obstructing stones can cause lasting renal damage if unrecognised.
pitfalls: Dismissing an isolated low serum urate as unimportant and missing the diagnosis
Failing to advise against strenuous anaerobic exercise in an at-risk patient
Attributing post-exercise acute kidney injury to rhabdomyolysis alone
Overlooking urate stones as the cause of haematuria
management: Advise avoidance of strenuous anaerobic exercise, the classic precipitant of exercise-induced acute kidney injury in this disorder
Encourage sustained good hydration to reduce urate crystal formation, stones and haematuria and to protect the kidney during exertion
Treat episodes of exercise-induced acute kidney injury with rest, fluid resuscitation and supportive management, avoiding further nephrotoxic insults
Consider peri-exercise antioxidant strategies to counter the loss of urate as a circulating antioxidant
Monitor for urate urolithiasis and nephrocalcinosis with renal tract imaging and manage stones accordingly
Confirm and characterise the transporter defect by SLC22A12 (URAT1) and SLC2A9 (GLUT9) sequencing and provide genetic counselling
Follow renal function longitudinally to detect lasting injury from recurrent acute events or obstructing stones
